title: Essay
prompt: Write an essay that, if everyone read it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.
final_prompt:
Write an essay that, if everyone read it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Deliver the result as one Markdown file, working in the current directory.
- Save it in ./output/ under any name ending in .md (for example ./output/essay.md). ./output/ must hold
  exactly one .md file; anything else there is ignored.
- The file is published as it is and shown as a page: headings, paragraphs, lists, block quotes, emphasis,
  links and code blocks. No raw HTML (it is shown as plain text) and no images that need other files.
- Keep it under 200 KB.
- Keep notes, outlines, drafts and any scripts outside ./output/ (in the working directory or a
  subdirectory): they're published as the source.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you wrote.

output.title: Everyone Else Is Reading This Too
output.excerpt: An essay written on the assumption that it will be read by everyone. The premise I was given is strange, so let me take it seriously. Suppose this essay really were read by everyone. Not by the people who already agree with it, not by the people with time to read essays, but by everyone: the woman…

runs.summary: Everyone Else Is Reading This Too is an essay arguing that a piece everyone reads could do the most good by correcting what people believe about one another. It draws on research on pluralistic ignorance to show that most people are more honest, moderate and cooperative than they assume, and it explains what that misperception costs and which small actions could change it.

output.title: To Everyone, at Once
output.excerpt: An essay written for every person alive This essay was written for everyone. Not for everyone who agrees with me, or who speaks a certain language, or who reads a certain kind of book. It's for every person alive. So as you read it, picture who else is reading it. Your mother. Your neighbour. The…

runs.summary: To Everyone, at Once is an essay of about 6,000 words written for anyone, anywhere. It uses the fact that everyone reads the same text to spread life-saving knowledge, from home-made rehydration for diarrhoea to seatbelts and vaccines, to correct false beliefs people hold about one another, and to offer plain advice on how to live well.

output.title: Make It Possible to Say Something Is Wrong
output.excerpt: A child breaks a cup. An adult hears the crash and comes into the kitchen. There are now two things to deal with: the broken cup, and what the child is learning about bringing this adult bad news. The cup is easy to see. The second thing may matter for decades. The adult can teach care with fragile…

runs.summary: Make It Possible to Say Something Is Wrong is an essay of about 2,000 words on making honesty safe, holding power to account and making repair practical, from family life to public institutions.

output.title: A World That Works on a Bad Day
output.excerpt: A good society should be possible on a bad day. When you have slept badly. When someone you love is ill. When you are frightened, distracted, or wrong. When you cannot find the words, cannot afford the journey, cannot understand the form. We often imagine progress as a world full of better people…

runs.summary: A World That Works on a Bad Day is a 1,921-word essay on building a society where dignity, safety, and help are within reach of ordinary, fallible people. It asks what a world should look like for someone who is having a hard day, not just for someone at their best.

output.title: How to Be a Little Less Wrong, and a Little More Kind
output.excerpt: An essay about the two skills — thinking clearly and treating people well — that make almost everything else better. What kind of essay helps the most people? Before saying anything useful, it's worth being honest about the assignment itself. If the goal is to improve the world for the greatest…

runs.summary: How to Be a Little Less Wrong, and a Little More Kind is an essay arguing that the greatest good comes from two universal skills rather than any single cause. It shows readers how to hold beliefs in proportion to the evidence, by seeking out critics and asking what would change their mind, and how to treat others as fully real, from assuming honest mistakes over malice to asking before accusing and forgiving.

output.title: Being Wrong, Cheaply
output.excerpt: There is a particular half-second that decides much of what happens to us. It is the moment just after you discover you were wrong. A fact lands. The name you were sure of, the number you quoted, the judgment you made about a person, the plan you defended in a meeting. For a fraction of a second…

runs.summary: Being Wrong, Cheaply is an essay arguing that human progress depends less on how rarely people make mistakes than on how cheaply and quickly they can find and correct them. It examines why admitting error is socially costly, how uncorrected errors compound, and what the aviation, medical and forecasting cases teach. It closes with seven practical habits for making correction easier, from pre-mortems and public rewards for changing one's mind to plain apologies.

output.title: The Person in Front of You
output.excerpt: Most of the harm people do to one another is done by people who believe, in the moment, that they are justified. Not by the rare monster who enjoys suffering. By the parent who is tired. The official who is owed a favor. The neighbor who heard a story. The driver who is late. The crowd that would…

runs.summary: "The Person in Front of You" is an essay that sets out a few everyday duties people can reasonably expect of one another: treating each person as real, pausing before harm or rumor, repairing what one has broken, raising children without hitting, telling the truth others rely on, and doing the easy rescues that keep people alive. Its closing lines are written to be read aloud.

output.title: The Skill of Being Wrong
output.excerpt: A short essay about the one habit that, if everyone practiced it, would improve nearly everything. Why this essay exists Almost every large problem humans face is not a problem of resources or intelligence. We have enough food to feed everyone. We have enough energy technology to avoid the worst…

runs.summary: The Skill of Being Wrong is an essay arguing that epistemic humility is a practical, learnable skill and perhaps the highest-leverage idea for the greatest number of people. It makes the case that certainty is a feeling rather than evidence, that strong opinions are best held weakly and tested in disagreement, and that honesty builds the trust cooperation depends on, closing with a handful of daily habits.

output.title: The Unglamorous Work
output.excerpt: Nobody is coming to fix the world. That is better news than it sounds. Somewhere in early adulthood, most people make a discovery that rearranges everything and that almost nobody says out loud: there are no adults in the room. You find out that the people running the hospital, the ministry, the…

runs.summary: The Unglamorous Work is an essay of about 5,000 words arguing that the world's worst problems are no longer mainly a shortage of knowledge but a failure to act on what is already known. It breaks that gap into four points, where people fail to see the truth, trust one another, reach those nearby, and weigh the long term, and it offers a week of small, mostly unseen habits that repair each one.

output.title: A More Good World Is a Practice, Not a Miracle
output.excerpt: The world’s problems are often described as if they were one enormous problem. They are not. There is no single evil to defeat and no single solution waiting to be discovered. There are billions of decisions, layered within institutions that reward some behaviors and punish others, producing…

runs.summary: A More Good World Is a Practice, Not a Miracle is an essay arguing that a better world comes from ordinary, coordinated moral habits rather than grand gestures. It covers preventing avoidable suffering, strengthening institutions, protecting truth, widening participation, and making beneficial choices the default, with practical principles for action at personal, civic, and global scales.

output.title: The Next Person
output.excerpt: A better world is not waiting for a better species. It is waiting, in part, for people like us—distracted, frightened, generous, inconsistent people—to make one small change in how we move through a day: treat the humanity of others as real, especially when it would be easier not to. This sounds too…

runs.summary: The Next Person is an essay arguing that widespread improvement starts with seeing others' full humanity in ordinary moments. It offers practical guidance on using power responsibly, telling the truth, setting boundaries without cruelty, repairing harm, helping in ways that widen others' freedom, and acting on the world's problems without being paralyzed by their scale.

output.title: The Next Person You Meet
output.excerpt: The driver who cut you off this morning may have been careless. He may also have been rushing to a hospital, half-asleep after a night shift, or lost in a grief so fresh that the road had blurred. You do not know. I do not know. Yet most of us decide in half a second: idiot. The cashier is slow…

runs.summary: “The Next Person You Meet” is an essay arguing that the world improves when every person is treated as fully real. It makes the case for holding first judgments lightly, choosing small kindnesses that multiply across billions of lives, repairing mistakes quickly, and leaving people, places and the future a little better than they were found. It ends with five practices for the next encounter, along with a call to extend the same mercy to oneself.
